title: Green Fingers and Green Thoughts

paragraphs.text: Gardening is not just a pleasant thing to do on a Saturday afternoon, or a way to minimise one’s supermarket bill, though both are perfectly valid justifications for doing it. Gardening is an activity that engages with core philosophical questions concerning, among other things, such mainstream ideas as human wellbeing and wisdom. That is why philosophers should take a closer look at the gardens they will find growing in almost every community. Perhaps the first thing to notice about this activity is the enormous amount of labour that still goes into it, despite technological advances that have transformed other activities: disinfecting the greenhouse; transporting the compost; buying, plainting and watering the seeds. Philosophers may be forgiven for wondering, as they do, why people go to all this effort. A first response is that gardening gives us pleasure, like lying in the sun or eating an ice cream from a shop. There are of course great pleasures in gardening – the clematis in bloom, the taste of a fresh, ripe tomato you’ve just picked – but they are short-lived and not necessarily more intense than other weekend activities like watching movies.

Here, though, we are thinking of happiness purely in terms of pleasurable feelings. However, there is an older idea of contentment which philosophers have recognised since Ancient Greek times. This is less about sensual pleasure, and more about peace of mind. In other words, planting seeds and watching them grow develops characteristics like patience and persistence in gardeners, leading to a deeper feeling of contentment than just short-term pleasure, and this helps explain the popularity of gardening.

Gardening, however, has further attractions, because there also seems to be an artistic element – whether it is arranging a small backyard or designing a great public park, the principle is the same. Works of art are usually put into certain categories and, in the tradition of the philosopher Immanuel Kant, we can compare gardeners to more conventional artists, except their materials are flowers and trees rather than brushes and colour. And certainly, gardeners have always displayed enormous powers of imagination.

Further, even through the activity of the suburban gardener may appear unusual to some, gardens fill the Earth. Looking at gardening across cultures, there are patterns to be seen and sociological conclusions to be drawn. On a local scale we can see this in neighbourhood events and national celebrations. Flower and vegetable competitions, as well as blossom and harvest festivals, can be more than temporary diversions; they give a feeling of belonging to a certain place.

What is more, in numerous traditions, gardens are seen as representing the philosophical debate of the time. The gardens of the French Renaissance period for example, in their formal structure, were inspired by the philosopher Descartes’ ideas about symmetry and space, which were then popular. The Garden of Cosmic Speculation in Scotland was a response to developments in scientific cosmology. Successive generations have been inclined to use gardens in this way.

Various past philosophers have noted these aspects of gardening – and more – but one gets the sense that the garden is just starting to be taken seriously again as a subject of intellectual inquiry. It is an exciting tine to be a gardening philosopher or a philosophising gardener. Other, it takes a ground-breaking book or essay to make philosophers and intellectuals see the important nature of a new field of inquiry, and this is certainly the case with Professor David Cooper’s recently published A Philosophy of Gardens, which has had a significant impact on the debate.

Recently, there has been a wealth of new ideas about the philosophy of gardening. For example, the historian Helene Gammack has described how the great European households of the seventeenth century attempted to cultivate the majority of food they consumed. Gammack argues these principles of self-sufficiency and autonomy have had a revival in modern times, when vegetable gardens are often found at both large and more modest houses in many western countries. A quite different set of ideas was evident at the royal palaces of the ancient Eastern Mediterranean, with their scented flowerbeds and exotic water features. These gardens were designed to display the strength ana conquests of the kings to whom they belonged. Also interesting is the legacy of General Lafayette, a hero of the American revolution in 1783. During visits to America to see his former commanding officer George Washington, Lafayette shipped thousands of seeds and cuttings back to his garden in Frances, because he wanted to give visual form to the ideals of the American Revolution.

Research conducted at the University of Georgia focuses or the way gardens are places where we can become enchanted by the magical and mysterious fusion of man and nature. According to this view, gardens are often designed to bring out a sense of wonder in those who experience them. The philosopher Mara Miller observes that gardeners do not work to a conventional clock. Instead their time is intimately linked to the rituals of an annual calendar; the time to plant out seedlings, to harvest, to make compost from fallen leaves. Finally, the now ruined garden of the fifteenth-century Mexican poet King Nezahualcoyotl illustrates a feature common to all gardens: the opportunity they afford their creators to explore and demonstrate their own personal ideas and obsessions. In all of these different ways, then, it is clear that gardening can inform philosophical enquiry into fundamental questions about human life.
